title: Functions
description:
## Functions
Functions is the core of Haskell, with it being called a _functional_ programming lannguage. Functions are defined as follows:
```haskell
<func_name> :: <type_signature>
<func_name> (params) = <code>
```
func_name is the name of your function, and code is code / a `do` block.
Type Signatures look somthing like this: `(Arg types...) -> (Ret type)`. If you had a function that took no arguments (later), and returned nothing but preformed IO, your signature would be `IO ()`. _Looks familier, doesn't it?_. If you had a function that takes two Ints and returns a Int, it's type sig would be `Int -> Int -> Int`.
Arguments are basically variables temporaraly defined when a function is called then dissapere when the function ends. After making a definition like `Add :: Int -> Int -> Int`, you could define the arguments like this:
`Add A B = <code>`, where A and B are the argument names.
Returning is the value sent out of the function. The last statment in the function is the value returned, so to finish our demo `Add` function, to add the two arguments we could do this:
```haskell
Add :: Int -> Int -> Int
Add A B = A + B
```
Calling functions executes the code in functions. To call a function you just do `<func_name> (args)`.
## Show
Show is simple, it just converts what you pass as a argument to a string, so `show 10` returns "10"
## Warning
Functions and variables in Haskell MUST start with a lowercase letter
